title: 2 Ways to Fail Your Child
author: Michael Keller
summary: Michael Keller argues that Christian parents tend to fail their children in one of two opposite directions when raising them in a smartphone-saturated culture that puts, in his words, every child in Manhattan. The 'Bunker' strategy of control walls children off from the culture, forgetting that sin lies inside as well as outside and producing 'hothouse flowers' unprepared for the real world. The 'Bubble' strategy of avoidance keeps the peace by placing few limits and skipping hard conversations, which teaches children that faith is optional; Keller cites Christian Smith's finding that parents' religious seriousness is the strongest predictor of a teen's faith. Drawing on Jeremiah's letter to the exiles in Babylon, he proposes a third model, the 'Embassy,' a home that lives inside the culture under a different constitution. Its operating manual holds that culture is created good, deeply broken, and in need of redirection, yielding a practical method of affirming, critiquing, and redirecting, illustrated with a conversation about Frozen. He closes by reassuring parents that imperfect execution is expected and that modeling calm engagement with hard questions is itself formative.
points: Bunker parenting delivers truth without grace, sealing children off from culture and leaving them unequipped to handle doubt or disagreement by adulthood.
Bubble parenting delivers grace without truth, and Christian Smith's research suggests children inherit a vague 'moralistic therapeutic deism' when parents model little seriousness.
Keller's Embassy model, drawn from Jeremiah 29, asks families to engage and serve the surrounding culture while operating by different loyalties.
His three-part manual (culture is good, broken, and redeemable) becomes a repeatable method: affirm the longing, critique the distortion, redirect toward a better answer.
Using Frozen, he shows how ordinary media can become formation, noting the film's own resolution rests on self-sacrifice rather than self-expression.
quotes: There are two ways to fail your child, and they move in opposite directions. You can fail by keeping too much out. You can bring up a child so isolated from anything that goes against your faith that by age 18 she has no means of coping with a world that doesn’t agree with her. When she meets a compelling false idea, how will she know how to wrestle with a doubt if those have never been discussed? How will she be able to explain what she believes to someone who disagrees with her if she’s never had practice doing it, or even seen anyone else do it?

You can also fail by letting too much in. You can be so afraid of being labeled as one of “those weird Christian parents,” or want to keep dinner peaceful, that you end up treating your faith like a private matter not worth mentioning. You avoid filtering what your kids watch or listen to because you’re not going to be one of those legalistic religious types. So you skip the hard conversations. But kids get the hint: Christian faith is an optional preference. It’s not important.

Now, thanks to smartphones, every child in America is basically living in Manhattan. They may not walk through Times Square, but they scroll through it on their phone. All culture is right there in their pocket.
The Bunker creates hothouse flowers. These kids look healthy in temperature-controlled, windless environments, but they aren’t ready for the weather of the real world.

The sociologist Christian Smith found that the single strongest predictor of a teenager’s faith isn’t youth group attendance or church involvement. It’s the religious seriousness of his or her parents. Children rarely surpass what they observe growing up.
The Bunker and Bubble strategies both fail, though for opposite reasons. The Bunker gives a child truth without grace. The Bubble gives a child grace without truth.
You’re not banning the movie, but you’re not blessing it either. You’re teaching your child to think. This is how you build spiritual antibodies.

When you know the operating manual of the embassy, you don’t have to panic when your kids bring home confusing questions about identity, sexuality, meaning, justice, or morality. Instead of shutting down the conversation out of fear like the Bunker parent, or ignoring the moment like the Bubble parent, you can slow down. Affirm the longing behind the question. Identify the distortion in the cultural answer. Point toward the hope that Jesus is putting the world back together, and your child with it.
